title: Usage delta restorer with fast-path checkpointing
creator: Maya Patel
description:
Problem: We frequently need to reconcile short-lived ingestion gaps (missed events, transient connector failures, schema hiccups) without running full tenant-wide backfills. Full replays are expensive and risky for high-cardinality tenants. Goal: build a "delta restorer" service that can apply compact, time-bucketed deltas for a tenant with a fast-path that uses checkpointed snapshots and progressive validation before committing to downstream aggregates.

Scope: incremental restore controller + worker pool, checkpoint snapshot store, two-mode execution (dry-run/commit), streaming assertion hooks for schema and metric drift, cost estimation engine for operator guidance, console integration for issuing restores and observing progress. This ticket covers the controller, fast-path heuristics, and console API changes. Workers and longer-running reconciliation adapters are follow-ons.

Design highlights and trade-offs: 
- Checkpointing: we will capture lightweight tenant snapshots at daily boundaries (keys: tenant_id, snapshot_id, watermark). Checkpoints are intentionally shallow (high-level counters + a small digest) to keep storage and comparison cheap. Full state snapshots would be too heavy.
- Fast-path vs slow-path: small delta sets (<= 10k events or <1% of tenant daily volume) will use an optimistic apply path that streams validations and commits in micro-batches. Larger deltas trigger a throttled slow-path with staged reconciliation and tenant-scoped quotas.
- Idempotency and ordering: delta tokens are strictly monotonic per-tenant. Workers use the token and a short-lived lease to prevent double-apply. Operations are idempotent via a multi-key op-log entry per micro-batch.
- Validation: progressive assertions run on a sampled subset of records and on derived metric sanity checks (monotonic counters, retention window checks). Failure in validation rolls back the micro-batch and escalates to slow-path or human review.
- Cost control: an estimator simulates token counts and approximate compute cost before starting; the console shows an estimated cost and time. Operator must acknowledge for predicted cost > $X.

API and UX: 
- Console: new "Restore" flow on the Analytics > Data Health page with selectable time-range, tenant scope, preview dry-run, and cost estimate. 
- Backend: POST /api/analytics/restores -> returns restore_id. GET /api/analytics/restores/{id} for status stream. 

Integrations and artifacts: 
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ANALYTICS/Delta+Restorer+Design+and+Safety+Model
- Initial PR for controller scaffolding: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/2431
- Runbook draft: https://docs.redwood.ai/runbooks/analytics-restore

Acceptance criteria: 
- Controller can accept and persist restore requests with tenant-scoped checkpoints.
- Fast-path micro-batch worker applies small deltas end-to-end in dry-run and commit modes with progressive validation.
- Console shows dry-run preview and cost estimate, and operator can trigger commit.
- End-to-end test coverage for idempotency, validation failure rollback, and lease expiry handling.

Risks and mitigations: 
- Risk: optimistic apply could corrupt aggregates on a subtle schema change. Mitigation: conservative default sample size for assertions + automatic rollback on any assertion mismatch.
- Risk: high-cardinality tenant accidentally selects commit and incurs large cost. Mitigation: require explicit acknowledgement and a soft quota that forces slow-path.

Next steps and rollout plan: 
1) Implement controller and checkpoint store (this ticket).
2) Implement worker fast-path and dry-run tooling (sub-issue ENG-995002).
3) Console UX and cost estimate exposure (sub-issue ENG-995003).
4) Pilot with internal ops and two low-volume customers.

Estimate: 5 points (controller + checkpoint store + API + tests).
